title: Moduli morphism of a finite locally free affine groupoid
statement: Let $k$ be a field, $U=\operatorname{Spec}E$ and $R=\operatorname{Spec}L$ affine $k$-schemes, and $(U,R,s,t,e,i,c)$ a groupoid over $k$ with $s,t$ finite locally free. Put $C=\{a\in E:s^\sharp(a)=t^\sharp(a)\}$, $M=\operatorname{Spec}C$, and $\mathcal Z=[U/R]$. The invariant inclusion $C\hookrightarrow E$ induces a canonical morphism $f:\mathcal Z\to M$. This morphism is uniform categorical, quasi-compact, quasi-separated and a universal homeomorphism. For every algebraically closed extension $\Omega/k$, the induced map $\pi_0(\mathcal Z(\Omega))\to M(\Omega)$ is bijective. Moreover $\mathcal O_M\to f_*\mathcal O_{\mathcal Z}$ is an isomorphism. More explicitly, for every flat map $\operatorname{Spec}C'\to\operatorname{Spec}C$, the equalizer of the two maps $E\otimes_C C'\rightrightarrows L\otimes_C C'$ is exactly $C'$, and this is the ring of global functions on $\mathcal Z\times_M\operatorname{Spec}C'$. These assertions allow empty schemes and variable rank. Algebraic stacks and quasi-coherent sheaves have the meanings in [def-sfb-adequate-moduli-space], and algebraic spaces have the meaning in [def-trf-algebraic-space]. A 2-fibre product retains the specified isomorphism between the two images of an object. For an affine groupoid $(U,R,s,t,e,i,c)$, the groupoid laws are those of [def-a1-scheme-groupoid-laws]; $[U/R]$ denotes the fppf stackification of the groupoid with objects $U(T)$ and arrows $R(T)$ on test schemes $T$. The point space of an algebraic stack consists of field-valued objects up to isomorphism and common field extension, with topology detected by a smooth surjective scheme atlas. A morphism is a universal homeomorphism if every base change by an algebraic stack induces a homeomorphism of these point spaces. Quasi-compact means quasi-compact inverse images of affine scheme tests, and quasi-separated means quasi-compact relative diagonal, both on scheme charts. A morphism $f:\mathcal Z\to M$ to an algebraic space is uniform categorical if, for every flat algebraic-space map $M'\to M$ and every algebraic space $T/k$, composition with $f_{M'}$ is a bijection from $\operatorname{Mor}_k(M',T)$ to $\operatorname{Mor}_k(\mathcal Z\times_M M',T)$. Flatness is tested on scheme charts using [def-weil-flat-morphism].

source.place: Tags 0DUM (lemma-well-nigh-affine), 0DUP (lemma-well-nigh-affine-moduli-space) and 0DUR (lemma-moduli-space-finite-affine); the flat equalizer assertion is groupoids.tex Tag 03BK (lemma-invariants-base-change), and geometric points are lemma-points (Tag 03BL).

proof.text: By the flat groupoid quotient/open-presentation theorem, $\mathcal Z$ is algebraic, $a:U\to\mathcal Z$ is representable finite locally free and surjective, and $R=U\times_{\mathcal Z}U$. For maps into an algebraic space, viewed as a discrete stack, a functor from the groupoid is just a map from $U$ equalizing $s,t$: compatibility on arrows is equality and all coherence is unique. The stackification universal property extends this functor; uniqueness is checked locally on $U$ because every object locally lifts and the target is a sheaf. Thus maps out of the quotient are exactly invariant maps. The map $U\to M$ induced by $C\hookrightarrow E$ equalizes $s,t$, hence descends uniquely to $f:\mathcal Z\to M$. For an affine $k$-scheme $T=\operatorname{Spec}B$, a map $\mathcal Z\to T$ is an invariant map $U\to T$. By the affine spectrum correspondence it is exactly a $k$-algebra map $B\to E$ landing in $C$, equivalently a unique map $M\to T$. This proves the categorical property for affine targets, for every groupoid under the hypotheses of the item, without assuming any moduli theorem.

Let $C\to D$ be flat. The affine flatness criterion identifies this condition with flatness of $\operatorname{Spec}D\to M$. As $C$-modules, $0\to C\to E\xrightarrow{s^\sharp-t^\sharp}L$ is exact. Flat tensor exactness gives $0\to D\to E\otimes_CD\rightrightarrows L\otimes_CD$ as an equalizer, so the invariants of the base-changed groupoid are exactly $D$, under $d\mapsto1\otimes d$. The affine fibre-product formula identifies its atlas and arrows with $U_D,R_D$. The pulled-back atlas covers the algebraic stack $\mathcal Z_D$, with self-relation $R_D$ by associativity of $2$-fibre products. Part (2) of the fppf-presentation theorem therefore identifies $[U_D/R_D]$ with $\mathcal Z_D$. Apply quasi-coherent algebra descent to its structure algebra: its global sections are this invariant ring, hence $\Gamma(\mathcal Z_D,\mathcal O)=D$, with the indicated structural map. On affine etale tests of $M$ this is exactly the value of $\mathcal O_M\to f_*\mathcal O_{\mathcal Z}$ by the definition of direct image. These identifications commute with restriction because every map is induced by the structural ring maps. Therefore the canonical sheaf map is an isomorphism. Step 1 also gives affine-target categoricity after this flat affine base change.

source.place: Tag 03BK (lemma-invariants-base-change), flat case; global sections by groupoid descent.

proof.text: For algebraically closed $\Omega/k$, every object $z\in\mathcal Z(\Omega)$ lifts to $U(\Omega)$: the scheme $U\times_{\mathcal Z}\operatorname{Spec}\Omega$ is nonempty finite locally free over $\Omega$. Its nonzero finite-dimensional coordinate algebra has a maximal ideal, whose residue field is finite over $\Omega$ and therefore equals $\Omega$ (each element satisfies a polynomial, which splits over $\Omega$). Such a point includes the isomorphism to $z$. For $u,v\in U(\Omega)$, the identification $R=U\times_{\mathcal Z}U$ identifies their isomorphisms in $\mathcal Z(\Omega)$ with arrows of $R(\Omega)$. The existing orbit-fibre lemma says precisely $U(\Omega)/R(\Omega)=M(\Omega)$. Hence $\pi_0(\mathcal Z(\Omega))\to M(\Omega)$ is bijective. This argument includes nonreduced finite covers and uses no etaleness of $s,t$.

source.place: Tag 03BL (lemma-points), geometric points; finite atlas from Tag 0DUM.

proof.text: The invariant-integrality lemma gives $E$ integral over $C$, so $U\to M$ is integral, hence universally closed by the integral/affine/universally-closed equivalence. For any affine scheme $T\to M$, write $U_T=U\times_MT$. The map $U_T\to\mathcal Z_T$ is surjective. If $D\subseteq|\mathcal Z_T|$ is closed, its inverse image in $|U_T|$ is closed, and its image under the closed map $|U_T|\to|T|$ is exactly $f_T(D)$. Thus $f_T$ is closed. Step 3, applied to algebraically closed fields over residue fields of $T$, shows that $f_T$ is bijective on point spaces: two representatives over the same point can be compared over a common algebraically closed extension and then are isomorphic. Therefore $f_T$ is a homeomorphism. For arbitrary algebraic-stack $T\to M$, choose a smooth surjective scheme atlas and cover it by affine opens. The same geometric-point argument gives bijectivity. Images of closed subsets pull back to images under the already proved affine-test homeomorphisms, by surjectivity of points of $2$-fibre products. They are closed on the atlas and therefore closed in $|T|$. Continuity follows from stack point topology. Hence $f_T$ is a homeomorphism for every algebraic-stack $T$.

source.place: Tag 0DUP (lemma-well-nigh-affine-moduli-space), universally closed and universally bijective paragraphs; geometric-fibre argument using Tag 03BL.

proof.text: For an affine test $T\to M$, $U_T$ is affine by the affine fibre-product formula, hence quasi-compact. Its continuous surjection to $|\mathcal Z_T|$ makes that space quasi-compact: pull back any open cover, take a finite subcover, and use surjectivity. Thus $f$ is quasi-compact by the stated affine-test definition. The relative diagonal is representable because $\mathcal Z$ is algebraic. Its base change by the surjective flat locally finitely presented scheme cover $U\times_M U\to\mathcal Z\times_M\mathcal Z$ is $R\to U\times_M U$. Both schemes are affine, so this map is affine. The representable fppf-locality lemma, applied to $\Delta_f$ and property affine, makes $\Delta_f$ affine. An affine map is quasi-compact and separated by affine-morphism permanence, hence has quasi-compact diagonal. Consequently $f$ is quasi-separated: its relative diagonal is quasi-compact and quasi-separated. Covering and representability are preserved under the indicated base changes; the cover here is the product of two base changes of the finite locally free atlas.

source.place: Tag 0DUP, quasi-compactness paragraph; Tag 04XD (lemma-check-property-covering), relative affine diagonal.

proof.text: We prove uniqueness for maps to any algebraic space $Y/k$. Suppose $h_1,h_2:M\to Y$ have equal composites with $f$. Their equalizer $H=M\times_{(h_1,h_2),Y\times_kY,\Delta_Y}Y$ is a scheme because the diagonal of $Y$ is representable. Its map $e:H\to M$ is a monomorphism and $f$ factors through $H$. After every scheme base change of $M$, $e$ is injective on points and surjective, the latter because $f$ is surjective. Also $\mathcal Z\to H$ is surjective on points. For every closed subset $F$ of such a base change of $H$, its inverse image in the corresponding base change of $\mathcal Z$ is closed; its image in the base change of $M$ equals $e(F)$ and is closed by step 4. Thus $|e|$ is a homeomorphism. The closed-embedding-affine lemma makes $e$ affine, so $H$ is affine. The affine-target property in step 1 supplies $r:M\to H$ with $rf$ the given factorization. Uniqueness for the affine target $M$ gives $er=1_M$; monicity then gives $re=1_H$. Hence $e$ is an isomorphism and $h_1=h_2$. This proof applies after every flat affine base change, by step 2.

Let $g:\mathcal Z\to Y$ and $p\in M$. The affine etale-neighbourhood lemma applied to $U\to Y$ gives an affine $V$ etale over $Y$ such that $W=U\times_YV$ is a scheme and $W\to U$ is surjective, separated, etale and locally quasi-finite. Pull back the groupoid to $V$, obtaining arrows $R_W=R\times_YV$ over $W$, with finite locally free source and target. Choose $w\in W$ mapping to $p$. Its orbit is finite because the source is finite, and the finite-set-affine lemma puts that orbit in an affine open of $W$. The existing locally-free-groupoid invariant-affine lemma gives an invariant affine open $O$ containing the orbit of $w$. Its arrow scheme $R_O=s^{-1}(O)=t^{-1}(O)$ is finite over affine $O$ and therefore affine. Write $N=\operatorname{Spec}\{b\in\Gamma(O,\mathcal O):s^*b=t^*b\}$. The morphism $(O,R_O)\to(U,R)$ has cartesian source and target squares: before restriction they are the base-change squares over $V\to Y$, and restriction to $O$ preserves them because $O$ is invariant. Its stabilizer square is cartesian as well: an automorphism of a lifted object is exactly an automorphism of its image, since $Y,V$ have no nonidentity arrows. The invariant etale-comparison lemma gives $N\to M$ etale and $O\simeq U\times_MN$. The source cartesian square then identifies $R_O\simeq R\times_MN$. Now $O=U\times_MN$ is the pulled-back atlas with self-relation $R_O$; part (2) of the fppf-presentation theorem gives $[O/R_O]\simeq\mathcal Z\times_MN$, and $p$ lies in the image of $N$.

source.place: Tag 0DUR, Existence and final two paragraphs, with Tags 07S0, 03JE and 0DT9.

proof.text: The map $O\to V$ in step 7 is invariant. As $O,V$ are affine, its ring map lands in the invariant subring defining $N$ and hence gives $N\to V$. This induces $h_N:N\to Y$ with $h_N f_N=g_N$ under the cartesian quotient equivalence. Repeating for every $p$ gives an etale covering of $M$ by affine schemes $N$. On an overlap $N_1\times_MN_2$, cover by affine opens. Each of these is flat over $M$, and step 2 gives the affine-target property for its pulled-back quotient. Step 4 and step 6, applied there, give uniqueness for target $Y$, so the two local maps agree on the overlap. Since an algebraic space is an fppf sheaf, the maps glue uniquely to $h:M\to Y$. The equality $hf=g$ can be checked on the pulled-back covering of $\mathcal Z$, or after the atlas $U\to\mathcal Z$; its restrictions are exactly the equalities just constructed. Thus $f$ is categorical for algebraic-space targets.

source.place: Tag 0DUR, Existence paragraph and final paragraph, spelling out the omitted gluing detail.

proof.text: For a flat affine $M_1\to M$, step 2 identifies its ring with the invariants of the base-changed finite locally free affine groupoid. Steps 1 and 3--8 apply to this groupoid and prove categoricity of $f_{M_1}$ for every algebraic-space target. For a flat algebraic-space map $B\to M$, choose an affine etale covering $B_i\to B$. Each $B_i\to M$ is flat. The just-proved property gives a unique $B_i\to Y$ for any given $\mathcal Z_B\to Y$. On affine etale covers of $B_i\times_BB_j$ uniqueness gives equality of the two maps. The sheaf property of $Y$ glues them to $B\to Y$, whose factorization identity and uniqueness are checked on the same covering. This is the required uniform categorical property, including all flat algebraic-space base changes. All prior arguments allow the zero ring and variable finite locally free ranks; the only nonempty finite cover used was the fibre over an object, where surjectivity guarantees nonemptiness.
